items.title: Simple vs. Compound Interest | Simple Beginners Guide

blocks.md:
Interest is the price of using money.

When you **borrow**, you pay interest. When you **save**, the bank pays you interest. It's like rent for money.

**Why does interest exist?**
If you lend money, you can't use it for a while. You also take a risk that it won't come back. Interest is the reward for that.

**Interest is usually a yearly percent**
A 5% rate means about $5 a year for every $100.

**Two sides of the same coin**
• On a loan, a lower rate is better for you
• On savings, a higher rate is better for you

Learning how interest works helps you on both sides.

Simple interest is paid only on the **starting amount**, called the principal.

**The formula**
Interest = Principal × Rate × Time

**Example**
You put $100 in an account that pays 10% simple interest a year.
• After 1 year: $100 × 0.10 × 1 = $10
• After 2 years: $100 × 0.10 × 2 = $20
• After 3 years: $30

The interest is the same every year, $10. It never grows on itself.

**Where you'll see it**
Some car loans and short-term loans use simple interest. Most savings accounts use compound interest instead, which grows faster.

question.prompt: $100 earns 10% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest is that?
question.explanation: $100 × 0.10 × 2 = $20. With yearly compounding it would be $21.

blocks.md:
Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Over time, it snowballs.

**Same $100 at 10%, compounded yearly**
• Year 1: $100 + $10 = $110
• Year 2: $110 + $11 = $121
• Year 3: $121 + $12.10 = $133.10

Each year's interest is a little bigger than the last.

**The Rule of 72**
Want a quick guess for how long it takes money to double? Divide 72 by the interest rate.
• At 6%: 72 ÷ 6 = about 12 years
• At 9%: 72 ÷ 9 = about 8 years

**Time is the secret ingredient**
The longer money compounds, the faster it grows. That's why starting early matters so much.
**It works on debt too.** Credit card balances compound against you. That's why unpaid balances grow so fast.

blocks.md:
These two terms look alike but tell you different things.

**APR: Annual Percentage Rate**
Used for **borrowing**. It shows the yearly cost of a loan, including some fees. Lower is better.

**APY: Annual Percentage Yield**
Used for **saving**. It shows what you really earn in a year, including compounding. Higher is better.

**Why APY can be higher than the rate**
If interest compounds monthly, you earn a little interest on your interest every month. So a 5% rate can give an APY slightly above 5%.

**How to use this**
• Comparing loans? Compare the APRs.
• Comparing savings accounts? Compare the APYs.
**Try this:** Look up the savings APY at two banks. You might be surprised how different they are.

question.prompt: Which number shows the yearly cost of borrowing, including some fees?
question.hint: The one used on loans and credit cards.
question.explanation: APR is for borrowing. APY shows what savings earn with compounding.

blocks.md:
**Fixed rate**
The rate stays the same for the whole loan. Your payment is predictable.

**Variable rate**
The rate can go up or down over time. Payments can change too. It might start lower, but there's more risk.

**Small differences add up**
On big loans, a small rate change matters. On a large home loan, 1% can mean thousands of dollars over the years.

**Smart moves**
• Shop around and compare rates
• A better credit score usually gets a lower rate
• For savings, move money to accounts with a higher APY
• Start saving early so compounding has time to work
